subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROFESSOR HUSON AND APPOINTMENT OF PROFESSOR CLARK

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROFESSOR HUSON AND APPOINTMENT OF PROFESSOR CLARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make in connection with the investigation of the United States old age insurance system. Yesterday afternoon the Minister of National Health and Welfare received word from Professor Gordon Huson of the
University of Western Ontario to the effect that, following the recent statement in the house by myself making it clear that the government wished to have a report on the United States old age insurance system in a matter of three or four months, he had reviewed the possibility of carrying out this assignment against the background of his university teaching responsibilities.
He indicated that while he felt it would have been possible for him to complete this study before the end of 1958, he could not, having regard to his university responsibilities, do so in the space of time contemplated by the government. In view of these facts Professor Huson has asked to be relieved of his responsibilities in connection with the projected study of the United States social security system. His telegram reads as follows:
In view of government desire to have pension report by early summer at the latest, may I please be relieved of my assignment to prepare it since my university teaching commitments must have first priority until the end of May.
This development is a keen disappointment, since Professor Huson was highly recommended. In view, however, of our sense of urgency in the matter of this study, we felt we had no alternative but to accept Professor Huson's resignation. In his place I am pleased to announce that Dr. Robert M. Clark, associate professor of economics at the University of British Columbia, has agreed to undertake this important assignment. Dr. Clark, who is a Ph.D. from Harvard University and is very widely recognized as an authority on this type of subject, has indicated that he is in a position to begin work immediately.

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF PROFESSOR HUSON AND APPOINTMENT OF PROFESSOR CLARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister if he has an assurance from Dr. Clark that he will be able to meet the deadline suggested by the Prime Minister the other day? May I also ask whether an examination has been made of the study of the system in the United States made by the old age security committee in 1950, and the other research material that has been collected since that time by the Department of National Health and Welfare? Is there not already sufficient information in the possession of the department to reach a decision on this important question?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: RESOLUTION REQUESTING CONVENING OF ATLANTIC CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the copy of this question which he had sent to me. The resolution on an Atlantic congress and Atlantic high level citizens' conference adopted by the third annual NATO parliamentarians' conference, the so-called Kefauver resolution, was in two parts. The first instructed committees of the conference to make arrangements for convening an Atlantic congress in 1959 in connection with the tenth anniversary of the North Atlantic treaty. That resolution requested heads of government to support this proposal at the NATO meeting in December.
The second part recommended that all NATO governments should, in consultation with the standing and political committees of the NATO parliamentarians' conference, 96698-236
Inquiries of the Ministry bring about a conference in 1958 composed of leading representative citizens to examine how greater co-operation and unity of purpose among NATO countries can best be achieved.
It was not found possible, Mr. Speaker, in the time available to consider the first part of this resolution at the NATO summit meeting in December. However, I assume that my hon. friend has in mind the second part of the resolution which deals with the bringing about of a conference in 1958. I would interpolate here that as a result of the meeting of NATO heads of government last December, a course has been charted toward even greater co-operation among NATO members in not only the military but also the political, economic, cultural and technical fields. I am personally optimistic that this unity of purpose and mutual co-operation, which has reached a degree unprecedented among free nations, will be strengthened.
I can assure the hon. member that the recommendation of the NATO parliamentarians' -conference-that is the second part of the resolution-is being given careful thought, and we are also investigating what support for the convening of such a conference may be expected from our NATO partners at the meeting of the council to be held next March. It is, however, premature to say what action will be taken in the council in respect of this matter at that March meeting of the North Atlantic council.

I desire to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that the question of local currency does not arise, because all UNRWA's aid is given directly to the refugees in the form of goods and services. There is thus no system of counterpart funds in local currency such as is the case in some other types of aid programs as, for example, under the Colombo plan.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the five minutes I had available to me last night before the house adjourned I had referred to the very large number of incorrect statements and errors of all sorts which had been propagated by the members of the three opposition parties as far as the farm price stabilization bill is concerned.

speechtext:
After five very long days of debate, under our present extended hours, on the second reading stage of the bill we had another example of the tactics which hon. members opposite follow, in that there were immediately two interjections after I had spoken for only five minutes. After five days of these outpourings from the opposition we had these two interjections, one by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano "filibustering his own bill", and the other from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate "a great way to get business done."
These foolish and childish interjections are typical, of course, of the sort of things which have been going on during this session, and which have been coming from hon. gentlemen opposite because they do not want to hear the facts. They feel they should have days and days in which to put forward their own misinterpretation of this piece of legislation, and when the minister responsible for the legislation attempts to reply they immediately try to prevent him from speaking by making interjections along these lines.
Last night, Mr. Speaker, I had pointed out that the main Liberal criticism of this bill was that it was not as good as the Agricultural Prices Support Act now on the statute books, and which the Liberals had introduced some years ago. I had indicated why I was quite sure that was a proposition which no farmer in this country would accept.
The other Liberal criticism of this bill put forward by the hon. member for Rosthern was that it does not cover wheat, oats and barley produced in the prairie provinces, which are handled by the Canadian wheat board. I think the reason for not including wheat, oats and barley under the price support act introduced by the Liberal government was that these grains were handled by the Canadian wheat board. The heads of the three prairie wheat pools did not want, and do not want now, to have wheat, oats and barley handled by the wheat board included in this bill.
3738	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
The reasons for their stand are very-obvious. If you attempted to handle these grains under two government boards the result would be nothing but confusion and difficulty. I feel there is no question but that it would destroy the efficient operations of the Canadian wheat board. Since the leaders of these three farm co-operatives who represent the people most directly concerned with handling these grains, and who I think know a great deal more about the matter than the hon. member for Rosthern or other members opposite, did not want these three grains included, it is rather difficult to understand why the hon. member for Rosthern and certain members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties have been criticizing the bill because these three grains are not included.
Whatever is done, so far as wheat, oats and barley are concerned, will be done under the Canadian wheat board, a body of which the great majority of western farmers are very strong supporters. I deplore the line taken in this regard, particularly from the point of view that it was an attempt to rouse sectional feelings so far as this bill is concerned. Time after time the hon. member for Rosthern said that this bill did nothing for the western farmers. This bill looks after every product produced by the western farmer, with the exception of wheat, oats and barley, which are looked after by another Canadian government board.
This attempt on his part to arouse sectional feelings in regard to this matter is a deplorable example of the extent to which he and the members of his party will go in order to try to stir up trouble in this country. One of the things, Mr. Speaker, from which we have suffered most in Canada is this business of the Liberal party trying to stir up sectional difficulties for their own political advantage. This was just another example of an attempt to do that.
The majority of the criticism levelled at this bill by the C.C.F. and Social Credit was merely abuse, abuse of me personally and abuse of the legislation. As such it is not proper, I think, to dignify it by answering it. Apart from this general abuse, the basic criticism of these two parties was that the legislation contained no rigid formula. This is correct. It contains no rigid formula for the very good reasons which I gave at the resolution stage, and again when I spoke on second reading.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization that all this bill provided for them was 80 per cent of the average prices for the past 10 years. As I have pointed out time after time, that is the absolute minimum guarantee in this bill in order to ensure what we might call a certain amount of ultimate security as far as the farmer is concerned.
The main purpose of the bill is to provide guaranteed yearly prices which can be set for any agricultural commodity except wheat, oats and barley produced in the western area. These guaranteed yearly prices, once they are set, will be in effect for 12 months in the future. In other words the bill brings forward prices into effect for the first time, and it provides to the farmer, through the ultimate security clause, through the guaranteed yearly price which will be put into effect-and which will be the one chiefly in effect-a very much greater degree of security than he has ever before enjoyed.

I know that the position of the small farmer is bad, but these members have tried to represent that if this bill were amended in order to put into it a rigid price support formula, it would help the small farmer and would look after his difficulties. As I pointed out in introducing the measure at the resolution stage, no one piece of legislation can be expected to solve all the difficulties of an extremely complex industry such as agriculture, and we of course were not so foolish as to try to do so in this bill or to try to represent to the farmers that it would do so.
This report makes several definite recommendations as well as conclusions, and I was talking previously about the conclusions. Mr. Chairman, I appreciate very much the privilege of saying a few words on the matter now before us. I had hoped to be privileged to speak on second reading but it seemed best not to do so. However, I appreciate the opportunity of presenting some of my thoughts at this time.
May I say that I have listened with considerable interest to a great deal of the debate on the bill. With much of what has been said I agree, but with some of the things that have been said I must say I cannot

agree. Many statements have been repeated many times. I expect that I will be repeating some of the points that have been brought out before, but because I represent people who have problems that differ somewhat from the problems of those in other parts of Canada, and because I have had some experience which I believe to be somewhat different from that of most hon. members, I am going to try to present at least one or two thoughts that have not thus far had much emphasis placed upon them. I do so in the hope that I may help to prepare the people of Canada for the changes I expect this farm bill will bring about.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that I have suggested that I think it will bring about changes. I say that because I have confidence in the bill and in the minister who is proposing the measure, and because I am confident that it will be possible to find men who will be willing and able to administer it fairly and honestly. I feel too that it is a special privilege to speak in support of a bill to assist agriculture. When I spoke some time ago I suggested that I thought it well to get started on the matter, and that while I did not expect the legislation to be perfect in every detail I did think it could be strengthened as it was found to be weak or defective.
I am pleased that as time has passed and some of the weak spots have been brought out the government has seen fit to recommend amendments. I think the minister is to be commended for his broadminded viewpoint in this connection. I wish to express my appreciation and pay my tribute to him as well as the department for his sense of fairness and seeming willingness to cooperate in giving the most sympathetic consideration to suggestions that have been offered by many members on this side of the house. To my mind that is something which speaks volumes for the agricultural policy of the government.
I believe this attitude on the part of the government and the minister in particular will tend to create the degree of soundness, strength and confidence in the agricultural policy of the government which it is going to need if it is to solve the problems that lie ahead.
I should like to take a few moments at this time to point out again that the region I represent has a great many problems because the farmers there produce a great variety of crops, and while the people engaged in the production of these crops represent only a small part of Canada nevertheless these matters are of just as vital concern to them as other problems are to people in other parts of Canada.

I feel that there is an indirect, if not a direct, reason why they should be encouraged to continue in the production of these crops in the interests of the general agricultural picture in Canada. That area of southwestern Ontario is very well suited to the production of quite a number of crops which, because of the climatic conditions there, cannot be produced to the same advantage in other parts of the country. I feel that for these reasons these people should be given encouragement to continue in the production of these special crops. Then the farmers in the rest of the country will not be faced with the keen competition which these farmers would afford were they discouraged from the production of these things and they directed their efforts into the more general lines of production carried on in most other parts of the country.
To illustrate my point a bit further, may I say that if the producers of such things as sugar beets, corn, tobacco, soybeans, white beans, tomatoes and so on were forced into competition with the producers of poultry, cattle, hogs and grain, it would make it just that much more difficult for the average farmer to survive.
I have in my hand, Mr. Chairman, a copy of a news letter published by the soya-bean growers' association in which it is stated that in 1956 the average price of soybeans was $2.16J per bushel; in 1957 the average was $1.96J or a difference of 20 cents per bushel.
I have in my hand also a copy of the latest Chatham newspaper which comes to my desk each morning. The price of soybeans as quoted in this newspaper is $1.90, a further reduction of 6 cents within the last few days. I point out these facts to show you that soybeans, for instance, are still on the decline, and to support the arguments I have so far advanced. May I say that I was pleased, in discussing with the minister this matter of agricultural policy in the light of this bill, to have been given the assurance that these special crops could be included in the designated commodities under the bill now before us.
It has been suggested that since only a relatively small number of people are concerned with the production of these special crops it does not matter whether or not these commodities are supported. My submission to this house is that if only a small number are affected, then only a small measure of assistance will be required to remedy their trouble. Since these people must share in the cost of whatever measures are taken to correct the problems of other areas, it is only fair that they should share equally in the benefits of those measures.

There is another very important reason why I feel support should be given to this bill. It is a reason which applies to all the people of our land rather than just to the farmers. If I may digress slightly for a moment, Mr. Chairman, in order to relate this point to the bill I would appreciate it. Some time ago we were discussing the passage of a bill of rights. I should like to suggest that if there is any one right the people should have in a country like ours, it is the right to expect good food. That is almost as important as life itself. I am one of those who believe that the food you eat will determine, to a great extent, what you will be. I feel I can speak with some authority in this connection because I have had the privilege of acting as an instructor in physical culture. I do sincerely believe in what I am saying, because I have practised it for a considerable number of years. I have faith in it. I have often said that what you eat, what you do and what you think make you what you will be. I believe that is true.
If I may, I should like to refer to a passage or two of scripture. It is recorded that the glory of young men is their strength. I suggest to you today that the glory of any person is his health and strength. It is recorded also that the body is the temple of the holy spirit, therefore glory God in your body. I do say that what we eat, what we do and what we think make us what we are.
These words will be of particular significance to all of us here, because it seems that when one is subjected to the strain, worry and responsibility connected with public service, the need for a strong constitution, a sound body and steady nerves cannot be overemphasized. I say these things in the hope that they may help to prepare the people of Canada for the changes I expect this bill will bring about.
If it is agreed that people have a right to expect the farmers to produce good food for them, then they should accept the responsibility that goes with that right to sufficiently compensate the producers of that food to ensure that they will not only be paid fairly for their labour but will be also in a position to maintain the fertility of the soil at a level which will enable them to continue the production of good quality food in the future. Thus they will avoid the necessity for mining their soil in an effort to get the last pound of food at the least possible cost, as it would seem the farmers have had to do at times in recent years.

Mr. Chairman, in my previous remarks I was endeavouring to point out that if the people of Canada had the right to expect the farm people to produce good food for them-and I admitted that I felt they had that right- they should be prepared to compensate the farm people fairly for the services connected with the production of that food. May I say that the scientists and doctors of our day- and by the way we have a number of doctors representing the people of their districts in our membership now-agree that in order to be at our best we require a certain balance of minerals, vitamins and so-called trace elements. When these properties are not found in sufficient quantities in our food they must be supplemented in our diet from other sources. That is all I intend to say on that subject.
I should just like to deal for a few moments with the bill itself. I should like to compare this bill with the old act in an effort to point out some of the advantages which this bill has and which the other one lacked, in my opinion. The old act is headed:
An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace.
To me it appears that in the heading of the bill-and I am referring to the old bill- there is an inference that it was only intended to serve as a medium of adjustment during that brief period when the economy of the country was being adjusted from a wartime to a peacetime basis. The old act has no preamble or statement of purpose. The old act definitely rules out one important crop from being brought in at all when it says "any natural product of agriculture except wheat". This had, in my opinion, the effect of discriminating against eastern wheat producers. Unlike the present bill, which names and guarantees support for nine main products, the old act did not provide any help unless a product was designated by the governor in council under clause (a) of section ' 2. The new bill does assure a definite guaranteed minimum of not less than 80 per cent of the average price received for the product over the last 10 years.
I feel that while the board-that is the old board; I am referring now to the old act- was given authority to operate, subject to the approval of the governor in council, there was no real obligation on the part of the board to carry on those operations because the act reads that the board "may" purchase agricultural products in the market. Apparently the matter of whether or not 

products were supported, and the price at which the support level was put, was entirely at the discretion of the board. I find also that there was no stated period for which the prices were to be maintained.
The new bill, on the other hand, not only provides guarantees in this connection but also provides for a minimum period of one full year during which assurance is given that the prices set will continue in effect. The old act gives authority for the board to appoint an advisory committee. The new bill, by section 5, provides that the minister shall appoint an advisory committee composed of farmers and representatives of farm organizations. Also the amount of money that is set aside to provide support for the products in question has been increased from the old figure of $200 million, most of which was never used, to $250 million.
I do not believe it is being contended that this bill represents a cure-all for the ills of agriculture. It will no doubt need further amending from time to time. That the government has maintained an open-minded attitude in the matter of making the bill sound and workable I believe to be a demonstrated and proven fact.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that in my opinion the success of a law does not lie entirely in the words that are written into it, but will require also men of sympathetic understanding, sound judgment and a sense of fairness in the proper administration of it to make it succeed. It is my hope that such men can be found who will be willing to serve. I greatly appreciate the privilege of speaking at this time in support of this bill.

I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he plan some game or games. I have in mind a game called "chum how" which would, I am sure, entertain farmers all over the country. I think these things are worthy of consideration.

The minister has taken credit for being open-minded, for not having fixed views, and I certainly would like to take advantage of that fact. I call as a witness the former member for Lake Centre, who is now Prime Minister, as he is quoted at page 5600 of Hansard for July 29, 1944. He said:
The farmer understands floor prices to be prices set at a level which will assure him of a reasonable profit over and above his cost of production, although some consider them to be the same as parity prices. Under this measure the board is empowered to make purchases, and to set the level of prices at which it makes purchases, regardless of whether that level may be below the level of the cost of production or not. [Mr. Johnson (Kindersley) .1

The farm organizations have been trying to get the minister to understand this, so he will incorporate the necessary legislative means to remedy the situation. The present Prime Minister went on to state:
But if this bill is to be anything more than a promise of a hope, there must be something in it to show that the prices the farmers are to receive will assure them of reasonable costs plus a fair return.
Mr. Chairman, I think that is worth fighting for. This is a principle which must be recognized by all hon. members and, indeed, many members have paid lip service to it. I maintain that if the Minister of Agriculture had invited the farm organizations to present to him draft legislation to stabilize agricultural prices, that principle would have been the first to have been written into the bill.
The minister has stated that he did receive representations from farm organizations. He most certainly did. The farm organizations were on their toes, taking advantage of the fact that there has been a change of government, hoping that things would be different and that they would be consulted. In fact they were consulted with regard to this legislation, but they were consulted after it had been introduced and after a storm of protest had been raised in the country and in the farm organizations because the measure did not include the principles which the present Prime Minister enunciated back in 1944. What we have advocated is a fixed base period, with a flexible application of the parity percentage to that base period, and there is all the difference in the world between those two. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture cannot differentiate between a fixed formula and a fixed base period to which you may apply a flexible application of a percentage of parity.
I wonder whether the Minister of Agriculture is as critical of the attitude of this leader as he is of the attitude of the opposition. Let me quote what the Prime Minister said on March 12, 1956, as reported at page 2021 of Hansard:
As far as parity is concerned, it must be related to a basic period which is regarded as one in which prices and costs are in approximate equivalence one to the other.
I know of no better definition of parity than that which appeared in yesterday's New York Times. I have made the necessary changes in the definition to meet the situation in this country. It is as follows:
"Parity prices are the dollars and cents prices that give to farm products the same buying or purchasing power they had in a selected base period when prices received by and prices paid by farmers were regarded as in good balance . . .
It has been put this way: If you can sell a truckload of barley and buy with the money received so much food, clothing, building materials, fertilizer, farm machinery and other living and production items as you could in a chosen favourable period in the past then your barley is selling at a parity price."
That was the definition of parity as applied to a fixed base period. He agreed with that himself, and then he moved this motion:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.

I am not worrying about it, I am merely answering these questions. This has all been of great interest to us, as I mentioned before. We realize this bill will do much for agriculture; we realize that in it there are many new measures which we are sure, when they are put into effect, will bring much benefit to Canada. We know that the ultimate security feature in this bill is the mandatory floor price on nine key commodities and that this factor is not provided for in the present Agricultural Prices Support Act. The setting of the guaranteed yearly price, one year in advance, to remain in effect for twelve months, is another important feature. We all realize that in agriculture we have to plan ahead and that in such long-range planning there are many factors which have to be considered, as I know from farming myself. I am sure that the twelve month period with certain guarantees will be of great assistance in this connection across the country.
There are some additional matters to which I would like to refer. The advisory committee composed of farmers is a new, democratic and sensible provision contained in this bill. We are sure that these people will be able to give to this government, to the department and to the minister concerned, much fine advice and the benefit of their wisdom and we feel sure the farmers of this land will feel that they have a true representation and true voice in the major decisions of the government.
The ten year moving average is another interesting matter and will also be of great value.
I will conclude my remarks by making a small plea that we should let this bill go forth to the country, and allow the people of Canada to decide as to its value. When they have done this, then let us judge it.

Mr. Chairman, the first matter to which I wish to bring the attention of this committee is the strange position taken by the Minister of Agriculture in connection with this bill. Having in mind the attitude taken by his leader during the time he has been in this house, and particularly during the last few years with respect to the rights of parliament, the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture is even more surprising. The minister introduced a resolution in the house and it was criticized. He then introduced a bill which was criticized in the country, as

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
we all know. We have also heard it was criticized by members of his own party. Then he suggested he was going to move amendments when we got into committee of the whole, and he actually told the house what those amendments would be.
By unanimous consent of the house, in order that the house would have before it the bill as he then thought he would actually ask for it to be passed, it was reprinted. In asking for second reading yesterday he told the members who were about to vote on second reading, "Of course, this bill is not necessarily the bill we are going to actually endeavour to have passed by parliament, because I intend to introduce still further amendments." He was asking us to vote for a bill while we were being told we would have further amendments introduced. We were asked to vote either for or against it without knowing what was going to be in the bill when it was finally passed.
Now if there could be a greater contempt of parliament, by insisting that it vote in such a way-blindfolded, in fact-I would like to know what it could be. On top of that, to make it even worse, we are twitted by members opposite because we do not know what the government is finally going to introduce in the way of amendments. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if the position were reversed, and the members of the present opposition had treated parliament with such contempt, and said "This is not the bill we ultimately intend you to vote on and have passed"; if the former minister of agriculture were asked what he had in mind and if he said, "I cannot say now," but insisted on a blind vote, I wonder what the present Prime Minister would have said if he had been in opposition. I wonder what would have happened if the previous government had taken such an attitude of contemptuous disregard for opposition members who are a majority of the members of this house.
I really was surprised that the present government should take such a position and say to us, "Oh, oh, you do not know what the bill is going to be." Here we are past second reading and the members on the government side are gloating because the members of parliament outside the Conservative party do not know what the government is finally going to bring in in the way of the legislation we will ultimately be asked to pass.

I would suggest to the members who gloat over that situation when parliament is treated with such contempt that they should think twice before they
speak, because in my opinion it is a shame and a disgrace that a party elected largely on the appeal for respect of the rights of parliament should have treated parliament in the way it has been treated in regard to this bill.
I think before we go any further it would be only fair if the Minister of Agriculture took us into his confidence and told us his intentions. After all, he is not running a dictatorship; he is sitting as a minister in a free parliament and we on this side of the house have just as much right to know what they want to be passed by this parliament as have his supporters. I repeat the request that he cease treating us with contempt and tell us what he intends to do.
This parliament has treated him with consideration by saying to him, "If you are going to change this bill by your proposed amendments, so much that it cannot be intelligently discussed unless we get a reprint, then the unusual course by unanimous consent can be taken of having such a reprint so that this parliament will have before it full details as to the bill." However, the minister says we will know of further amendments in his own good time and we are to vote before we know his intentions. This is very surprising coming from a government from whom we have heard so much and whose Prime Minister has insisted over and over again that he would restore the rights of parliament and the respect for parliament. We heard that from one end of the country to the other.
I ask the minister, is this respect for the rights of parliament? I ask the young members, who believe in the oratory and the high idealism expounded by their leader throughout this country, and who asked for the votes of the people on the strength of this plea to restore the rights of parliament, do they think parliament has been treated with proper respect in the way this bill has been handled?
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, that is the reason why about one-third of the members of the Progressive Conservative party did not see fit to vote for this government bill which is supposed to be such an important contribution to the welfare of the agriculture in this country. If they abstained because they believed in the words of their leader and because they would not support in this house the method of handling this measure which has flouted those words, then I say that those people who absented themselves showed a decent respect for the electors who elected them.

Was it because they did not like the way they were being treated; the contempt with which they were being treated by their own government? Or was it because they did not agree with the bill? Where were those hon. members on the government side? Why were they not here? This is a matter for which they have to answer when they come to speak.
Mr. Chairman, the minister tried to excuse the exclusion of all the grain growers of western Canada from the provisions of this legislation designed to help the farmers of Canada and stabilize their incomes at a fair level by saying that if some provision were made in the bill to pay money out of the consolidated fund toward raising the income of the grain growers of western Canada to a reasonable level this would destroy the wheat board. I have heard some astonishing arguments from members opposite in the short time they have been on that side of the house, but it seems to me that this argument perhaps takes the first prize for a really astonishing statement. The minister will remember that some years ago the Liberal government, feeling that the final payment to be made for wheat was too low, appropriated $65 million which it turned over to the wheat board in order to increase the final payment to the farmers at that time. Did hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in opposition, say that that would destroy the wheat board? I do not think they did. And did it destroy the wheat board? I do not think it did. I think it made the farmers feel that the wheat board was doing a better job, because this provision meant that they would get a bit more money than they would otherwise have received if this amount had not been turned over from the consolidated fund.
Why could not this government, when it was purporting to deal with the position of agriculture and improve the position of the farmer with regard to income, have included a special clause in this bill providing for the payment of moneys out of the moneys voted by parliament for the purpose of placing the western grain farmer in the position of receiving a fair share of the national income. This would not interfere with the marketing of grain in any way, as the minister well knows. It would merely ensure that the farmers growing grain in western Canada

would receive a fair share of the national income under the bill which the government has placed before us.
The minister went so far as to suggest that because we dared to speak for the people who sent us here and who trust us to represent their wishes we were raising regional cries. I think that is a rather astonishing attitude, coming from a minister from western Canada, when it is pointed out to him by members representing constituencies in western Canada that this bill, brought in by the government to meet the admitted needs of agriculture and give some help in combatting the cost-price squeeze, would exclude the grain growers of western Canada altogether. But because we brought that forward and said to him: you are leaving out these people who need help just as much as those in other branches of agriculture, the minister accused us of raising regional cries.
I just wonder what the people of western Canada will think about this attack on western members who dared to point out that the government, in this bill designed to help the farmers of all Canada, is certainly not helping them. And because we dare to bring this forward we are charged with making a divisive and regional claim. Is it making a divisive and regional claim for members from western Canada to ask for the same fair consideration for our farmers as is being given to other farmers in Canada? And is it not really something to wonder at that because we dare do that we are attacked for making a regional plea? Let the minister, when the time comes, answer for that to his western constituents.
Mr. Chairman, there is another matter with which I intended to deal. I do not wish to deal with any of these matters for any longer than is absolutely necessary to bring them to the minister's attention. I hear hon. members opposite laugh. One of the big problems facing Canada today is the present depressed condition of our farmers and the need to do something about it, and if this is regarded by members opposite as a laughing matter, then I hope they will be called to account by their farmer constituents whenever they dare to go to the country.
Mr. Chairman, we have been told that no one piece of legislation can solve all the farmers' problems. Admitted. But this was a piece of legislation which was held forth as having been designed to help the farmers in regard to the inadequate prices and income they are receiving. This bill was brought in for that very purpose. What is the use of saying, in these circumstances, when it is pointed out that it does not do anything for a large branch of agriculture

in western Canada, that you cannot expect everything to be done in one measure? I think the house has a right to expect that when a measure is brought in to help the farmers out in regard to their income, it should accomplish what it purports to do. There is nothing unreasonable about that.
When the government gets around to dealing with some other problem, let them deal with that new problem. But when they are purporting to deal with the income received by the farmers of this country, let them deal with that. Let them do it without half measures, without quarter measures and without repealing legislation which already protects farmers more than the bill the government is now bringing in. Let them deal with this problem and not hide behind the suggestion that they have not had time. It would not have taken any longer to have brought in an adequate measure to protect the farmers and give them a fair share of the national income than it has to bring in this present measure; in fact, it could have taken less time, because it would have met with the approval of parliament and would not have necessitated the long debate which this has aroused.
The government should pay attention to the promises on which it was elected and to the promises which hon. members held out when they were in opposition in this house. Attacks have been made by some of the younger members of this house upon the idea of fixing prices for farm products in the way they do in the United States. I would remind them that when the Liberal government pointed out that a system such as that followed in the U.S.A. was leading to the piling up of surpluses there, none were louder in their condemnation and ridicule of that position than some of the hon. members who are now sitting on the government benches. However, they held this out to the country, and got votes on that basis. But when the Liberals said that this basis of fixed parity prices would not work-let hon. members of the house remember this 

when we said that this was getting the government of the United States into trouble and injuring some of the farmers down there, all the arguments now being put forward by the Minister of Agriculture were met with derision by members of the Conservative party. Hon. members who do not know of that attitude should not be rising in their places and giving such enthusiastic applause to the sudden somersault of their leaders in this respect.

So far as I am concerned, this bill represents the most forward step ever taken by this parliament to meet the situation facing Canadian farmers. I have refrained from speaking previously on this matter for the reason that I want to see the measure placed on the statute books of this country in order to give the farmer an opportunity that he has not had in the past to the extent that he was entitled to a price in keeping with the cost of production.
It required a great deal of effort in the draftmanship of this bill to bring about what I hoped would be achieved and what I have advocated through the years, namely the assurance that the farmers of this country will be placed in a position under this legislation where each year, in respect of those commodities designated as coming within the ambit of this bill a price will be established before production starts so that farmers throughout this country will be closer to achieving a fair and a reasonable share of the national income.

Over the years I have seen the picture of agriculture developing in a way that required further and more action on the part of parliament. I am not going into statistics. I have before me a statement on agricultural policy made in 1957 which illustrates the situation as I saw it then and as I see it now. I join with the Minister of Agriculture in what he said this afternoon, that in our desire to achieve for the farmer a fair share of the national income we at the same time wanted to assure that if a major economic crash should take place there would be at least an emergency bottom beyond which prices would not fall in this country but at the same time there would be flexibility to permit this agricultural body as set up to listen to the advice of an advisory board composed entirely of farmers, and then to determine each year prices which would bring to the farmer a reasonable return.
My hon. friends of the C.C.F. party, in the attitude that they are taking, are doing their part with all the power at their command to deny to farmers throughout Canada the achievement of that objective which will be attained as the objective of this bill, namely the assurance of a fair and reasonable return, with the farmer knowing it in advance.
All of us know-and at the moment I am not going into any controversy on the question as to responsibility; I am simply stating facts-that since 1949 the costs of the goods and services which Canadian farmers have to buy have increased by 24.6 per cent while the prices of agricultural products have dropped by 11.65 per cent. A few years ago farmers as a whole received nearly 58 per cent of the consumer dollar. In the process of years that figure had fallen to some 50 per cent. There is a trend, and it has been a continuing one, whereby the farmer is receiving less and less, in relationship to the prices of the things he has to buy. That situation demanded action. What action could we take?
I discussed this matter with various farm leaders. If my hon. friends feel that throughout any part of Canada farmers do not today understand this legislation because of the fact that, through the attitude of the C.C.F. party in particular it has been misrepresented, the opportunity may not be too long delayed for the people to have the privilege of saying what they think of this legislation.

There are amendments to be made. We intended amendments to be made. We brought this legislation before parliament, first securing the opinions of those outside of the house. Subsequently helpful suggestions were made in the house. In addition to that, I have spoken to farm leaders over and over again. Amendments will be made to assure that the objective shall be declared to be to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income; that in every case the basic price will be determined upon the costs of production of the farmer; and that the advisory board to be set up will be required to meet a given number of times per year. These are changes that were made as a result of the representations of farm organizations which had been in touch not only with the minister and other members on this side of the house but with myself. This legislation if passed will permit the agricultural board to let the farmers across Canada know this year what shall be their minimum price during this present year.
Year by year farmers have represented, through their organizations, the need for such a flexible measure being established. That is being done under this legislation to the end that the farmer may know in anticipation each year what he is going to receive. Indeed the advisory committee-and I cannot anticipate in advance the sections-will consist of a chairman and of not more than nine other members composed of farmers and representatives of farm organizations. There is no suggestion whatever that this committee shall be composed of those adverse to a fair and reasonable deal for the farmer. They will make their recommendations. What more could we incorporate in a bill than that the recommending body should be one composed of those belonging to the class who are asking for those prices each year in keeping with a fair and reasonable dependence on the cost of production?
At no time did we suggest that the legislation will be perfect. Shortcomings in it will be found in the light of experience. Those shortcomings will be apparent as operation follows operation and in the light of experience. The objective is to give the farmers a fair share of the national income; in the fixation of the prices, regard will be had to the cost of production in so far as the basic price is concerned, which is a price which I might call an emergency price, in order to protect it from a general fall as a consequence of economic dislocation everywhere, not only in Canada, but throughout the world.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that a good deal of time today has been spent in discussing something which has been controversial, I am sure the house will welcome the opportunity to deal with a matter on which there is now virtual unanimity.
When I say that this bill to provide for a voluntary revocable checkoff has been introduced in every session since 1949, some hon. members may wonder why I should refer to it now as having support which is practically unanimous. Well, Mr. Speaker, there have been one or two changes since the bill was last dealt with in the house on January 29, 1957. However, on that occasion the bill had the support, not only of all the members of

Industrial Relations
this party and of all the members of the Social Credit party but also the support of most of the Conservatives who were in the house as well as the support of nine members of the Liberal party. It was defeated only because the majority of the Liberal party members at that time voted against it.
In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have moved over to this side of the house and, in addition to that, they have had another national convention. We have noted with interest the resolutions passed at that convention. One of them was to the effect that the Liberal party now stands for the enactment of the voluntary revocable checkoff of trade union dues. As a matter of fact, at the 1948 convention of the Liberal party the delegates went almost that far, although their resolution was in more general terms in that they asked for legislation to provide union security.
As I say, at the convention this year they have made their position more specific. They now stand for the voluntary revocable checkoff of trade union dues. In the light of that position I can only assume that most, if not all, Liberals will vote for this bill. The C.C.F. and the Social Credit parties will vote as they have voted on former occasions. At least I assume the Social Credit members will do so. As for our friends on the government side of the house, I would point out that included among those who voted for this bill last year are the present Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer); the Secretary of State (Mrs. Fairclough); the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton); the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green); the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean); the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith); the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) and the Minister of Labour himself (Mr. Starr). The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) was absent when the vote was taken on January 29, 1957. I made some reference to his absence while the vote was taken, at a meeting I addressed in Toronto a few days later. I did so because Hansard showed that the Prime Minister was in the house that day but was absent during the vote on this same bill. I must say that he came to me later, having seen that reference in the press, and explained to me that he was absent because he was recording a radio talk. He said that had he been here he would have voted for the bill, as he had done on former occasions. Mr. Speaker, that makes it unanimous, all four parties in the house are for it. So I guess I should not take any time talking about it; we might as well bring it to a vote and put it on the statute books.
What does it do? It provides for what is known as a voluntary revocable checkoff of trade union dues, which is sometimes referred to as the minimum form of union

security. Specifically, it provides that in the case where a union has been certified under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act that union may request that the employer deduct from the wages of the employees their union dues and pay them over to the union. However, there are still two further conditions. One is that even after a certified union has made such a request, the deductions can be made under this bill only in the case of those employees who actually sign cards requesting that their dues be so deducted. The other condition is that any such employee may at any time revoke his request; and if he does so, his dues will not then be deducted.
There are those who criticize this measure because it does not go far enough. This is, as I have already said, a minimum form of union security. I put it forward because it is that form of union security which has the support, as I have indicated, of all the parties in the house. It is precisely what is requested of the government by the Canadian Labour Congress. It is in a form which was drafted in the Department of Labour back in 1948 and which, for a few days in 1948, was in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that, in view of the change that took place on June 10, 1957, in view of the change on this question that took place in the Liberal party at their convention in January of this year, we should now bring to an end this long effort to write the voluntary revocable checkoff of union dues into our national labour code, and on that basis I present this bill to the house for its second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 152, REVISED STATUTES OF 1952    VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK- OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened, as usual, with great interest to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In his usual capable manner he introduced the bill. I am in a uniaue position. At one time I was not so heartily in accord with this bill as I am at the present time because I felt it infringed upon the right of the individual to determine just how he was going to work, who he was going to work for and with whom he wanted to identify himself in connection with his work. But since I have been dealing with the union as a member of a committee which was negotiating I was voted down, and I went very happily along with them. In a majority of instances, since the beginning of our dealings with the union, it has been left to me to make the agreement work effectively.
The reasons advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre covered a lot of the conditions that happened in the agreement but the term "voluntary revocable checkoff" is a misnomer. When the individual starts to work he has anywhere from 14 days to six months to decide whether he is going to identify himself with the union.
Another point is that there is never any checkoff in effect unless there is an agreement. Such agreements are arrived at by
Industrial Relations
negotiation. There is agreement to do certain things, and generally speaking it is a condition of employment that the workers must identify themselves with the union. As far as the term revocability, there is no such thing as revocability. Employees may revoke and withdraw their permission for their dues to be deducted under the pretext that they are going to pay them themselves but in the majority of cases that I know of that just does not happen. These people receive all the benefits the union can secure for them in the way of increases in wages and improvement of other conditions then want to renege.
In the case of the particular union I have in mind the only thing they had to gain was to bring up the wage scale after the war. The workers were receiving everything else that possibly could be secured for them by way of fringe benefits and conditions of work, holidays, pay for holidays and so on. But when some employees decided they did not want to have their dues deducted it was not very long before they were in trouble with the union because they had not paid their dues. As a result, they were suspended and I was notified they were no longer members of the union and they were then notified their employment was ended. The end result was that they could not revoke deduction of their dues and they had to keep on paying if they wanted to continue in our employ.
That brings us back to what is really involved, union security. It is definitely a matter of giving security to the union and I have always been in favour of it, though I was not present when the vote was taken. Had I been present, I would have voted for it. But since such legislation was first brought before the house in 1948 various things have happened. On some occasions the measure was withdrawn at the instance of the government because they did not want it on the statute books, but the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has reintroduced it year after year in the hope that it would be carried.
Since that time certain things have happened affecting the necessity for such legislation. The necessity first arose because there were certain employers carrying out federal government contracts who were not in accord with the idea. But that does not apply now because about 90 per cent or 95 per cent of the industries under federal jurisdiction operate under some kind of an agreement between the employer and the employees containing a similar checkoff provision or one providing even greater benefit. Therefore the urgency for the bill is not as great as it was then. As far as other industry is concerned, I would say there are very few unions that

Industrial Relations
do not have agreements with the companies concerned involving the checkoff or deduction of union dues.
In industries under federal jurisdiction, of 295,000 employees covered by collective agreements 235,000 have agreements that include the checkoff. There are 45,000 who have what is called the voluntary revocable checkoff and 191,000 have other forms of checkoff. About 59,000 are not covered in any shape or form and of those 35,000 are railway employees. Then there are some 16,000 working on ships or engaged in stevedoring and they have arrangements with their union hiring halls for collection of dues by the union.
Under these circumstances, the urgency for the bill is not quite clear at the present time although there is no reason why it should not be enacted when the principle is so generally accepted throughout the country. But there are considerable numbers of unions and a certain number of employers who just cannot go along with the idea, and I think that is the reason why this legislation has been introduced. These companies contend that it imposes certain bookkeeping and clerical work upon them that is not germane to their operations and which they think should be provided by the union because it is the union that will benefit.
To my way of thinking there are other things that enter into consideration of the matter at the present time. Six of the provinces already have such provisions in their legislation and they require that the principle be followed that the trade union must have the support of the majority of its members before deduction can take place. Arrangements for such deduction can be made under the legislation of those provinces. The six provinces are Alberta, British Columbia, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan and their legislation requires that the individual employee must authorize such deduction in writing.
In British Columbia, Newfoundland and Nova Scotia an employee may revoke at any time. Prince Edward Island does not provide for revocation. Saskatchewan removed the revocation privilege in 1951. The government of Ontario has had a standing committee studying the matter for some considerable time. In fact, the committee is sitting at the present time. They are trying to study how Ontario legislation can operate in such a way as to be of greater advantage to the labour organizations and also of management. There does not seem to be very much difference between labour and management except that in the case of a few organizations there is someone who feels that he has a vested right to keep himself

apart from being governed by such legislation as is now before us and these people reserve their right under our constitution to be free from any such checkoff arrangement. Eventually they will probably succumb to the reasonableness of deducting union dues in this manner.
There is also the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has invited proposals from the major labour and employer organizations, particularly those in the federal field, respecting the improvement and revision of federal legislation. Therefore the particular proposal now before us should be considered in conjunction with the proposals emanating from these organizations in respect of the general review of the legislation. That removes any immediate urgency for this bill because practically everyone is already covered.
There is also a general increase in the recognition of the importance of trade unions and their value in negotiating with employers. The value of these unions in negotiation cannot be overlooked because it makes for a happy labour relations with management, especially when the negotiation of the agreement avoids any unpleasantness or interruption in work. There are, of course, a few companies remaining who do not go along with this idea because they believe it saddles them with extra clerical work and accounting costs.
There are other matters in connection with this measure which may necessitate a careful examination from another angle altogether. Certain events have occurred within the last two or three years which probably make it necessary for us to be a little hesitant about instituting this measure. One reason advanced in favour of the bill is what is called union security, and that really means this is the easiest means of collecting union dues. I can remember the time when I had to go out collecting dues. The secretary and I would interview probably every member, and it was not such an easy task to collect dues. However, this was a craft union and we had practically everyone in it, and every member was paid up. Because we constantly called upon the membership we got to know the members very well and were always on friendly terms with them. The members had a good deal of confidence in their officers who were always in touch with the situation as it affected them.
Today, however, with the buildup of huge union funds, it is clear that the situation is altogether different from what it was when this bill was first introduced. Certain things were brought to our attention the other day which were dealt with very effectively by the

hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge). I do not want to go into them as exhaustively as he did on January 15, as recorded on pages 3377 and 3378 of Hansard, but I endorse practically everything he said. I refer to the matter concerning Harold Banks. The fact that such a situation exists in Canada I do not think is to the liking of any party in this house. I would say that I do not think any party would, for a moment, condone the procedure that has been followed down in Montreal. If hon. members care to read about it, they will find it all in Hansard. The dangers that are involved in unions having vast sums of money which can be brought under the control of certain individuals, are fully exposed.

It was January 15, page 3377. When one considers the general increase in the recognition of the importance of unions today, I would say that it is a very serious matter that confronts us. I would say that probably in the federal field there could be improvements in the act governing unions.
The point I want to cover was probably covered amply by an individual for whom I have very high respect. I have met him on only a couple of occasions, but he is a very capable labour officer. This article appeared in the December Journal of the Canadian Labour Congress and is entitled, "An Autonomous Labour Body". I would not say that the article is inaccurate, but the writer probably made some errors of judgment. As has been said, I think by Thomas Jefferson, where an error has been made there can be no great complaint about it as long as there is reason left to combat it. In so far as this particular case is concerned, I think the situation should be reviewed as it may affect Canada in the future. The writer is talking about Canadian newspaper comment upon the suspension of the international brotherhood of teamsters, chauffeurs, warehousemen and helpers of American Unions, and says that what takes place in the United States does not necessarily have to be followed in Canada. The article quotes Mr. Cushing, who states:
We see no reason why the Canadian membership of the union should be penalized for something that is happening the United States. If there was the slightest indication of improper practices on the part of the Canadian ranking officers of the union, then we would very definitely be concerned, hut there have been no such suggestions.
There is a question as to whether or not that is so, because in the newspaper last night there appeared this article with the following heading: "Teamster Chiefs Like Racketeers". The article reads:
Industrial Relations
Teamster union bosses were accused today of conduct "very similar to the protection rackets prevalent many years ago."
The charge was voiced before the Ontario legislatures committee on labour relations by spokesmen for the Automotive Transport Association of Ontario.
Earlier, the committee had heard from Canada's teamster boss I. M. (Casey) Dodds in person. But Mr. Dodds said he would present a brief only after hearing what the transport association had to say.
The brief was particularly scathing in its attack on the teamsters' technique of placing locals in "trusteeship" when they would not conform to the bosses' orders.
Two Ontario locals-one at Windsor and the other in Hamilton-were still in such a position, Dodds said, and U.S. labour czar James Hoffa was the trustee.
Dodds, appointed as administrator of the union by Hoffa, but never elected by teamsters in either Canada or the U.S., said Hoffa had not interfered with either local.
The fact remains that there are two unions in trusteeship to Mr. Hoffa. This places the statement made by Mr. Cushing in an entirely different light. I have not the slightest doubt but what Mr. Cushing does not go along with this point of view. I believe he is imbued with the same altruistic propensities as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). They do not condone or go along with these ideas. If one reads these labour journals, particularly the one that was issued last November as well as the issue of December, one finds that they are virtually textbooks for labour operations, and are very good. They contain a lot of valuable information upon which one can place reliance and implicit faith. The individuals writing the articles are people for whom I have the highest personal respect. Some of them are my personal friends of long standing, such as Russel Harvey and Mr. Archer. These are gentlemen with whom I got along exceedingly well in the past, and I know that they would not condone these conditions.
Then, too, Mr. MacDonald has covered racketeering in the labour movement very thoroughly. He has placed himself in a position where his services should be secured if we are considering future legislation in connection with labour racketeering. He has given a very fair summary of what has taken place in racketeering in the movement. He does not try to gloss over certain things that have taken place. He brings them out. Then he goes on to say this, and I will quote it. This is to be found in the November, 1957 issue:
At the same time, it must be remembered that racketeering is the exception rather than the rule in American labour. Ineptness is more likely to be found than corruption. There is an innate indisposition to malpractice in unions because of their very nature.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the substance of this bill. Before we find ourselves in a position

If labour is going to have any success, and it is coming into its majority very soon and there is a very critical time ahead for it in its organization, then those people who are in control of administration will want to make sure, as we will want to make sure, that everything in Canada is in order as far as the operation of our unions is concerned.	*
Therefore, in connection with this particular bill with which I am in hearty accord, I nevertheless want to know just exactly what is going to be done to see that those who are in control in the United States should not get control here. I think that is what should be the crux of this legislation which is before the house, but before I go along with it I would like to have the assurance of those in whom I have the utmost confidence that what has happened in Montreal during the last three or four years is going to come to an end, and that some means will be found to see that these individuals are responsible not only to the union but to the people of this country.

I was interested to read the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Macdonald) with respect to human rights. I would like to know how we will

assure that the human rights of the individual will be made to apply to the men in the unions who have found themselves enmeshed and encompassed in the goings-on of some labour leaders.
I would like at this time, in case hon. members think there is no seriousness in this matter, to give to the house a rough summary of a sermon preached by Cardinal Spellman when he was talking to the soldiers who had returned to New York from overseas service. He said that they would find some of the things which they had been fighting for were non-existent in their country today and he touched upon the condition of labour. He described situations where soldiers returned to take over their places in civilian life in the United States and where some segments of that country had fallen under the ruthless domination of greedy and godless gangsters and murderers whose aim was to force management and labour alike to be the twin slaves of the underworld. He mentioned the sordid details of corruption and violence which were daily features in the newspapers and the close association of some union leaders with known criminals, the creation of dummy locals, the rigging of elections, extortions, acid-throwing, graft and misuse of union funds. Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment briefly upon the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) about the voluntary revocable checkoff of union dues. Because of its implications, a proposal such as this invariably arouses much interest in labour circles-of whom I am personally a representative. I feel therefore that this matter should be thoroughly studied before a conclusion is reached.
As a general rule, it might be better to leave any decision in this matter in the hands of labour unions and let labour and management come to an agreement. However, at times, in spite of any amount of negotiation, labour representatives cannot come to an agreement with management. In such cases, legislation such as this would certainly be of great benefit to labour.
At every session of parliament since 1949, a private bill similar to the one now before the house has been introduced by my hon. friend for Winnipeg North Centre to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, so as to include voluntary revocable checkoff of union dues. On many occasions it came to a vote, with results that have never been satisfactory to my hon. friend.
I should like to make a few comments on this Bill No. 5 so that hon. members may be in a better position to judge this proposed legislation.
While this bill rests on an acceptable principle, it is not without objectionable features. For instance the method used in making the checkoff would be comparatively weak. In fact, it could be divided as follows:
1.	-The checkoff is voluntary and requires the signature of each employee;
2.	-the checkoff can be revoked in writing at any time chosen by the worker concerned;
3.	

the checkoff applies only to the union, recognized as a bargaining agent, of which the employee concerned is a member.
A survey prepared by the statistics division of the Department of Labour shows that

collective agreements covering employees under federal jurisdiction contain clauses providing for union dues checkoffs in favour of the union concerned in a proportion which is at least equal, if not far greater, than that provided for by this bill.
Of the more than 294,000 employees covered by collective agreements in industries under federal jurisdiction, approximately 235,000 are covered by agreements which already provide for the voluntary check-off of union dues. Of these, only 45,000 are covered by collective agreements providing for revocable check-off. The other 191,000 employees are covered by collective agreements providing for some form of mandatory or irrevocable check-off of union dues. In most cases, the relevant clauses provide for the irrevocable check-off for the life of the agreement.
Of the 59,000 employees under collective agreements which do not provide for the check-off of union dues, 35,000 are railway employees who apparently have decided that this provision does not answer their purposes or desires.
Then 16,000 others are mostly water transport workers or dockers provided by the union with the necessary facilities for the collection of union dues.
As I have said, I agree with the principle of the bill. I believe that the clause providing for union dues check-off should be irrevocable for the duration of the agreement. When a worker signs his membership card, he knows of the conditions under which he agrees to work. Nothing forces him to sign and if he decides to do so, it is his duty to support his union at least for the duration of the contract.
In my opinion, no one is in a better position than the unions themselves to say what benefits best serve the interests of their members. They are closer to their members than we are, and they certainly are better able to judge what benefits they need most.
In some cases, labour unions, complying with the wishes of their membership, would prefer some other form of check-off or benefits other than the check-off.
I think that the adoption of the bill moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would set a precedent which we might regret later. I would not be surprised if, before long, the hon. member or some of his colleagues sought from parliament other
Industrial Relations
measures which might not be as desirable as we might think.
I am sure the hon. member will understand this point of view and I repeat that, while agreeing with the principle of the bill, I wish this matter to remain a bargaining point between workers and employers, that is to say between union representatives and employers. It seems to me that this way the interests of workers will be better served than by the passing of the bill moved by the hon. member.
