We will discuss that when we come to the individual clauses of the bill. I do want to make a few remarks with regard to some of the things which have been said by hon. members in various parts of the house during the time that this matter has been under discussion and which were more or less related to the bill. I did say in earlier discussions that there was some considerable difference in the title of this bill and the title of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The long title of the Agricultural Prices Support Act is:
An act for the support of the prices of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace.
I stated at an earlier stage in the discussion that it would be no surprise if it was intended, whenever the act was amended, and now when it is intended, to substitute another act for it, to change the title somewhat. The fact that we have come a considerable distance away from war would justify that expectation, but I was a little critical of changing the word "support" to the word "stabilize", and in some of the discussions which have taken place it has been suggested that stabilization was not intended in the previous act. I just wanted to call attention to the fact that section 9, subsection (2) reads as follows:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1), the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Therefore, it was intended in the Agricultural Prices Support Act-and as a matter of fact it was the practice-that stabilization be carried out under it. The support program which was set out in the original support act of 1944 did not just originate at that time; it was something that had been in effect more or less throughout the war and something which had come into being largely because of experiences not only in the last war but in previous wars. The experience in previous
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization wars had been to the effect that prices went up during wars, costs in general went up during wars, and at the end of the war there was the general inclination to speak of price conditions being in a state of inflation, and there was a very definite effort to strike at that inflation by some method or other. The usual practice over a long period of time had been first to attack food costs, clothing costs and costs of shelter; the idea being that if you could get those down to reasonable levels, then you could cut down wages, then you could cut down costs of commodities in general, and eventually get your price levels down to lower levels than they had been during the war period and immediately after.
During the last war there were many economists who took the position that that was something that was most difficult for farmers and for primary producers in general to stand at the end of wars and that therefore there should be an effort made to avoid that happening at the end of world war II. It had happened at the end of world war I, when everyone who was on a farm at that time now knows that those who went out and started in with livestock toward the end of the war, and bought breeding stock at high prices, found in a very short period of time, in a year or two, prices dropped down to a level where it was impossible for them to carry on.
The main purpose of the act of 1944 was to try to avoid having that happen at the end of world war II. If we had been trying to do that only in Canada I do not expect that we would have had very much success with it; but it was an effort that was being made in all of the allied nations, in Britain, in the United States, in European countries and in Canada. By all working at it I think we have, at least up to the present time, been able to accomplish the objective that we had in mind, namely to prevent prices being forced down to unusually low levels following the war. Therefore, in carrying on through the transitional period from war to peace I think the legislation has done some good for farmers throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
In addition to that, the legislation grew out of the fact that we had been doing this during the war. I hold in my hand a copy of the speech which I delivered in the house on March 9 and 10, 1942. This speech was delivered just about a month after the farmer's march was made on Ottawa in 1942, which has been referred to in this debate a number of times. That march was made by 400 farmers. Someone said the other day that it was more or less promoted and organized by friends of mine. I suppose there is
3778	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization some justification for that because the real leader, or the honorary leader, if not the real leader, of the delegation was the previous minister of agriculture, the Hon. W. R. Motherwell. He was along with them. The 400 came here and presented their case, first to the government as a whole, then to the wheat committee of the government, which at that time was composed of three or four members of council, and then they made their representations to others associated with agricultural activities here.
In reporting on that matter to the House of Commons at that time I called attention to the fact that their first request was that we should provide for parity prices of agricultural products. I referred also to the fact that I gave them to understand that I could not assure them the government would agree to such a policy; but I did assure them that I would present the whole matter to council as they presented it to me and report back to them later. That was done. When reporting to the house I pointed out that there had been something in the nature of support prices similar to those asked for in the period between the time that the delegates had been here or before they came and the time I was speaking, which I again state was in March of 1942. I am going to read only part of one paragraph in order to bear out what I have been saying and to indicate that something has happened to prices since that time.
From the very beginning of the war It was realized that if farmers in Canada were to be able to maintain themselves and develop agriculture to the point where it could take its proper place in providing food for allied countries, prices in due course must advance. Very early in the war we embarked upon a policy of trying to establish floors under various farm products. The first product under which we Were able to establish a floor was hogs. That floor was established by entering into an agreement with the British government in the fall of 1939, the first fall of the war. The second product under which we were able to establish a floor was cheese; it was established in the spring of 1940, when a price of 14 cents a pound at Montreal was agreed upon with the British government. No, excepting slightly in 1936. It started from 1936 and went up gradually until you come to the year 1939 when the war started, which is shown on the graph. It went gradually up until 1941. The war started in 1939. By 1942, the year about which I have just been speaking, the black line or net income had gone away up to two-thirds of gross income, leaving one-third absorbed by costs. From then on it has gone up gradually. It does drop down occasionally and then goes up again, but it went up gradually until it reached the peak of over $2 billion in 1951.
When members of the house start to talk about the agricultural position now they start up at that peak in 1951. Then they say it has dropped since. It did drop down for two or three years partly because of the $400 million drop in grain crop value in western Canada in 1954. The net income dropped down to less than half the gross income but since it has been coming back up again. It is true it has not reached the level it was at in 1951, but when one is making comparisons and trying to indicate that certain things have happened all I am suggesting is that one should not try to show that none of the improvement can be attributable to the benefits that came about during that particular time from the fact that we had the Agricultural Prices Support Act but that he should assign some part of them to the fact that we had that act. Perhaps we should not assign any greater proportion to the fact we had that act than is the case of other countries with similar legislation which made it possible for them to avoid allowing the farmer to fall into the same slump following the last war as happened in wars prior to that time. Therefore I think we should acknowledge that some good has been done by having the Agricultural Prices Support Act even though some members may not be inclined to say that it was just as helpful as it might have been or as it could have been.
To come back to the legislation before us at the present time, I have already indicated that stabilization was provided both
under the old act and in this bill. But there is one thing about which there has been considerable discussion, and I think the minister referred to it last evening when he began his final speech on second reading. I refer to the time period provided in the bill. The bill does provide for definite notice of one year; in other words, prices established must be continued one year at that level. I presume it is the calendar year although I am not sure about that.
Under the old legislation that was the practice in connection with most products. My hon. friend shakes his head but I am sure he has this document, entitled "Federal Agricultural Assistance 1942-1956", in his possession. I am not going to read it all but it does bear out what I have said. It is issued by the department and it indicates just what has happened in connection with all products over the years. It is true it has not been the calendar year in most cases because many of our products are produced on a different basis.
The hog year, for example, starts on November 1. This is due to the fact that over a very considerable part of this country the young hogs come in the early part of the summer, April or even in March in some areas. They are marketed about six months later. It is very cold in many parts of this country, so many of our hogs are produced in the summer months when it is easier to produce them. We have, therefore, the end of a production season coming along about November 1. It has been the practice, over most of the years, to start the floor price on hogs on November 1 and carry it through to October 31 the following year.
When it came to dealing with butter or with cheese, as every dairy farmer knows, the dairy year begins on May 1 and ends at the end of April the following year. The support prices have been for a 12-month period beginning with the first of the dairy year. On two or three different occasions the support price has been announced two years in advance. This book contains all the records of the years in which that happened. The first year, I think, was in 1951, at which time the price was set for two years in advance. This has been done on two different occasions since. As a matter of fact, we are operating on that basis now. The support price was set at 58 cents, and was to continue until the beginning of the dairy year in 1958 or until April 30, 1958.
If the minister is bound under the act to make it for only a year, then he cannot do otherwise. But we did find it preferable on some occasions to lengthen that period, depending on the conditions which existed at the time.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
Another suggestion that was made in discussing the question was that we have followed a practice-it is indicated that it may have been for all products-of simply setting one period at one time and another period at another time. Again I would warn the minister when he is amending some of these sections that there are certain things that cannot be dealt with a year in advance. I hope he will give that some consideration. For example, it is only two or three years ago that 85 per cent of the apples on the trees in Nova Scotia were blown off just at the time when they were ready to be harvested. No one could give consideration to that 12 months in advance and make provision for it. It had to be dealt with at the time.
The result was that one of the other ministers and myself got on a plane in the morning, after discussing the matter with the government the evening before, and we were in Nova Scotia at ten o'clock in the morning. We sat down with the government and the growers of Nova Scotia, some of our officials and some of their officials, and before night we had worked out a plan under which we took care of the 85 per cent of the apples that had been shaken off the trees. It was done in a simple manner. We said we would pay 90 cents a bushel for every bushel of apples gathered in boxes and put in piles. This was done under this act, but it could not be spread over a 12-month period. You could not pay them for 12 months before. You simply had to act under the legislation that gave you the authority necessary in order to deal with a situation of that kind.
I have said this before, and I am going to repeat it now that so many new members are here, that was the most satisfactory and most acceptable plan I was ever able to carry out in the 22 years I was in the government, if one takes into consideration the way it was received by the people concerned. It was the only thing I did in 22 years in connection with this act or any other act about which I did not have a single complaint. The real reason for that was that we decided the money should go directly to the farmers concerned. It did not go to the people who supplied the apple barrels, the people who supplied fertilizer or the other things the farmer had to get in order to produce a crop. We paid the 90 cents a bushel into the hands of the farmers. Ninety cents a bushel does not sound like very much, but I believe the apple growers in that area were very well satisfied, as the Minister of National Revenue would tell you if he were here. It was quite satisfactory to an organization for which he had been solicitor over a considerable period of time.

I am only saying that you cannot write into a bill something of this kind that binds you to act only in some certain way. I would think from the wording of the clause, and I am going to say something about that later, such action would be possible under the clause as it is. If it is not, then I am quite sure the minister would agree that something should be done about it to make it absolutely certain he is not bound. We carried on, in connection with all the products mentioned here to which it might be applied, on that basis.
The one product mentioned in this bill with which we did not carry on very long was cattle or beef. We had a very good reason for that. The reason was that we have the best market in the world for our surplus beef, and that is the United States. We always took the position, and the federation of agriculture agreed with us, that it would not be a good thing to put a support price under cattle because we had that market. We could ship our surplus there, and we could get the best price. If we set a price which was higher than the United States market price, our market would be flooded with beef. If the price were lower, we would be told that the government was putting down cattle prices. If these things occurred, we would very soon have to change the price. We could not wait until the first of the next year in order to change it; we would have to do something about it.
I am suggesting to the minister that he not tie his hands too closely on a thing of this kind, so that it would be impossible to do many of the things he will find it absolutely necessary to do as he goes along. Under the old act we did do practically what the minister is suggesting should be done under this bill. Nevertheless, after the experience we had, we would never have written into an act that that was what we had to do. We simply said that we had authority to do it. Then all the facts were taken into consideration at the time and whatever was necessary was done.
That is all I want to say about the measure itself. We can discuss most of these matters on the different sections. However, I do want to say something with regard to the remarks that have been made concerning the attitude we have taken on this measure, and the reasons we have given for taking that attitude. I gave those reasons about December 20, I think it was. After giving them, I stated unless there were some material changes in the bill between that time and the second reading stage most members on this side of the house would be inclined to support second reading. We had that vote today and I think that undertaking was carried out. I heard some on the other side, however, who were

referring to the fact that we were not all here. I have been here now for 22 years and have noticed that most agricultural matters have been dealt with on Thursday and Friday. I do not know just exactly why. It is probably because those are the days on which there is the poorest attendance in this house because hon. members who live rather close to Ottawa go home. Those of us who come from Prince Edward Island, which is almost entirely a province of fishermen and farmers; those of us who come from the prairies, where it is almost entirely agricultural, and even going out to British Columbia where there are fishermen and farmers, have to be here whether we like it or not. I presume that is one of the reasons why it has been customary to have these matters discussed on Thursday, Friday or Saturday.
Hence there is a good reason as to why there were not as many members here today as there might have been at any other time. As a matter of fact, I was a little bit surprised last evening when the minister did not allow this matter to go to second reading at five minutes to six because we would have had a better attendance than we have today.

In any event it was for that very short period of months only. That was what was done in most cases. Otherwise if a commodity was put under price support, it was put in without any date being mentioned so that it could therefore be cut off like that at any time, and nobody was in a position to complain about it. Thus there was no forward pricing provided for in the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and in the application of that act forward pricing, by and large, was not made use of. There is only one thing in the bill, an expression of fear that you must not do anything because if you ever give the farmers a decent price they are going to produce so much they will choke themselves to death.
Would anybody believe that high prices will produce surpluses? I do not, and I should know because I am a practical farmer and, according to the hon. member for Melville, a successful farmer. I always find that if I can get good prices for my products I can live like other people and work like other people. I can work 10 hours a day instead of 18. If I get good prices I will take some of my land out of production and put it into grace to preserve it for future generations. These are things I can do only when I have obtained good prices for my products to cover the cost of production that is parity prices. These are the things for which I am asking. If I do not


get them, then I have to go and plough up every slough and produce as many bushels as I possibly can in order to make a living.
I want to say that even the government does not believe that good prices produce surpluses. This is just empty talk. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture made a statement the other day -I had it here but somehow I lost it; anyway, it is right in Hansard-that when the farmers receive low prices they are automatically forced to produce more in order to make a living. This makes sense. I believe that. If that is so, then why be frightened at giving the farmers a price that at least pays their cost of production; that is all they want. This is all they mean when they talk about parity prices.
I want to tell you this. One thing this country needs, if it needs anything, is more production. There is nothing more certain in my mind than that within five years this country will be short of several major farm products. This country will go hungry. Yes, this country will be short of meat, milk, butter, eggs and cheese. As a matter of fact, we are short right now. Take butter for example; we are only producing half as much as we should. The only thing that saves us from eating dry bread is the fact that we have margarine. Why then are we worrying about over production?
Then, let us take meat as an example. I know there are a lot of people who do not realize this fact, but here is the situation. This is a statement which appeared in the Financial Post of July 14, 1956, not quite two years ago:
For over a year we have brought into this country more beef or beef cattle than we have shipped out.
Why do we worry about surpluses? The former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, made this statement one day when he was speaking to the Ontario federation of agriculture:
-beef production is no longer surplus, and all evidence is that beef production may not meet the demand over the next few years.
This man knew we would have no surplus, and he admitted it. Here is another statement, made on January 24, 1957 by the minister of agriculture for Manitoba:
In 20 years time, if present per capita consumption rates are to continue, Mr. Shuttleworth said, farmers will have to prepare 1,300,000 more cattle for market each year, produce an additional 365 million gallons of fluid milk and turn out increased quantities of butter, cheese, poultry and eggs.
Why are we frightened about giving the farmers a decent break? Let us take milk as an example. There is no doubt in my mind that we are going to have a milk shortage

I should like to say a few words on this clause. As I think I have stated on the occasions on which I have spoken on this bill, the purpose of my participation in the debate is to improve the bill. As we come to clause 2 (1) (a) wherein are given the definitions we come to an extremely important aspect of this bill. I noticed that earlier in the debate this afternoon the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, in relating this bill to the Agricultural Prices Support Act, made a great point of the fact that the Agricultural Prices Support Act ruled out wheat, something which he claimed was a discrimination against the western wheat producer. He then went on to praise the action of this bill. But, Mr. Chairman, this bill specifically excludes wheat, oats and barley grown in western Canada.
I think hon. members of this house appreciate the importance of western agriculture. I think they appreciate the amount of our western acreage which is devoted to the production of wheat, oats and barley. In fact, in western Canada last year a total of over 40 million acres were devoted to the production of those crops out of a total acreage of 104 million acres. We can therefore get some concept of the importance of wheat, oats and barley in the western economy.
At the same time, in the Manitoba CoOperator of January 2 I noticed a news story indicating that the drop in grain marketings hits Canadian farm cash income. I respectfully suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it will be impossible to fulfil some of the aspects of the bill. It will be impossible to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income, as the minister is proposing to do in one of his later amendments, without, in fact, providing the opportunity for including wheat, oats and barley in the act, or at any rate, not specifically excluding them.
This problem has been recently highlighted by the request of the western pools for a

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization deficiency payment to meet the cost of production. In the Western Producer of December 12 I find a report of a statement by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. It states:
He advocated a system of deficiency payments to offset the cost-price squeeze. Such a system should be paid back to the 1955 and 1956 crops, to equalize farm income.
The president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool went on to state:
The system would apply to such- farm commodities as hogs and livestock, in addition to grain.
I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that it is impossible to stabilize agricultural prices in Canada without stabilizing agricultural prices for the western grain producer. If we are going to allow legislation which, in fact, is discriminatory,-and that was proven by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent in the exclusion of prairie-raised wheat, oats and barley-I think we have a highly objectionable feature; and I think it is understandable that efforts should be made to have this aspect corrected.
The whole problem of western agriculture is one that revolves around the grain surplus and the marketing problems with which we are confronted. I think the Prime Minister is fully acquainted with this problem. Surely the Minister of Agriculture, coming as he does from Alberta, is also well acquainted with the tremendous surplus of wheat which we have in western Canada. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has been vocal on many occasions in connection with the surplus of wheat which we have in western Canada. It is apparent from the low deliveries which we have. Again in the Western Producer of December 19 we find a statement of the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool at the rural development conference held at Regina on December 10. He states:
Even with the sale of more produce today farmers won't have enough to carry on,-
We have there an indication of the necessity of some situation whereby we can hope to correct the cost-price squeeze confronting western farmers. We must have the possibility whereby we can bring in legislation to assist farmers who are indeed on a very low quota. In the Wheat Review of December, 1957 I notice that as of January 6, 1958 there are still 895 marketing points in the western provinces on a one-bushel quota; 887 are on a two-bushel quota and 256 are on a three-bushel quota. It is thus apparent that it is impossible for farmers to meet the cost of production on the basis of those limited deliveries.
I do not think it is the intention of any hon. member of this committee unduly to

hold up proceedings. On past occasions I think that I and other western members have dealt with this wheat aspect, and it should be unnecessary further to convince hon. members from western Canada of the necessity and the desirability of including western wheat, oats and barley within the act. I think that all western members will appreciate the fact that an amendment in this respect will improve the act. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie:
That lines 14 to 19, both inclusive, on page 1 of Bill 237 be deleted and that the following be substituted therefor:
"(i) any of the following commodities produced in Canada, namely, cattle, hogs and sheep; butter, cheese and eggs; and wheat, oats and barley; hereinafter called 'named commodities'; and"
I think hon. members will readily appreciate the effect of this amendment. It is simply to remove from the act the discrimination which is placed in it by the words "not produced in the designated area as defined in the Canadian Wheat Board Act". I am certain that the hon. member for Rosthern will come to my assistance in having this amendment passed by the house.
I should be equally certain, but I must express some doubt, about the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek who has been supporting the government with respect to this legislation but, appreciating the large wheat-growing area in his constituency, I think we will have their interests at heart. I think this would apply with equal validity to all hon. members from western constituencies and that the adoption of this amendment will be one step further along the road to improving the bill.
The Minister of Agriculture has already indicated there are going to be nine amendments made to the bill, which he states are for the purpose of improving it. I have moved the tenth amendment for the consideration of hon. members of this house and I am certain that the passing of this legislation will assist western agriculture to achieve some of the stability it deserves.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS, ETC.
speechtext:
When this amendment is moved that the governor in council is to be

guided by certain factors, it seems to me that the objective towards which he is to be guided should be put there too. As I understand it, the minister intends to move an amendment to the preamble to the effect that the purpose of the bill is to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income. As has been pointed out, that purpose is a part of the objectives section of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. When it appears in the preamble it has not a binding effect upon the board administering this act, it is just a vague objective. But if it is put into the operative section of the act as an objective of the act when prices are being set, then the provision has a more binding effect, and in this regard the measure becomes at least as good as the Agricultural' Prices Support Act. But if it is left in the preamble it is not as good.
I know it is no use my moving this as an amendment, but I would suggest to the minister that between now and when we meet again he should give consideration to adding at the end of the word "relevant" in subsection (ii) the following: "In order to provide that the farmers receive a fair share of the national income" and thus prescribe that objective as part of the objective in setting the prices. Then the minister could amend the preamble as proposed. It would certainly do no harm there, though it would not have any binding effect.

subtopic: CHAUDIERE RIVER, QUE.  REPORTS OF EXPERTS
CHAUDIERE RIVER, QUE.  REPORTS OF EXPERTS
speechtext:
1.	Have reports of experts been laid before any department of the federal government since 1917, regarding the overflowing of the Chaudiere river, in the province of Quebec?
2.	If so, (a) to what department; (b) by whom were they signed; (c) on what dates were they presented?
Answer by:	Mr. Hodgson, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Public Works:
1 and 2.
The Chaudiere river has been overflowing its banks and causing damages to varying extents practically every year since 1917. Departmental records indicate officials of the department were asked from time to time to report on the extent of the flood damages, to comment on the causes of this flooding and to suggest remedies. However, no comprehensive report on the whole problem has ever been presented to the department by other departments, either federal or provincial, or by any outside firm.
This matter has been studied extensively by the Quebec streams commission which has jurisdiction over such matters in the province of Quebec.
